Robert E. Lana examines psychological theory from a historical and epistemological perspective. He presents a history of the major epistemological ideas that are either implicit or explicit in psychological theory. A review of psychological thought from the Greeks to the early behavorists includes the work of such thinkers as Descartes, Locke, Hume, Kant, and James. Machiavelli, Vico, and Nietzsche are presented as key figures who contributed the major ideational structures that paved the way for the Freudian revolution.

Research and Experimentation in Psychoanalysis

Introduction

In this issue Modern Psychoanalysis presents in its research and experimentation section three articles in response to Kirman's theoretical paper on the application of modern psychoanalytic principles in educational settings.

Theodore Laquercia assembled a special class in the high school of which he was principal. The anecdotal material presented here is excerpted from a longer paper.

Richard Friedman reports on an informal experiment he conducted at an urban community college.

Dolores Welber offers notes and case materials based on her experiences with children in the elementary grades and their parents.

Larry Miller  

This book is written for the professional person engaged in the psychotherapy of individuals. It combines three essential ingredients that any book of this genre should include: (1) It describes the psycholocial needs of the human being from birth to death; (2) it

141

reviews the dynamics and etiology of the major psychosocial disorders (neuroses, psychoses, character problems, additions, and sexual deviations); and (3) it provides nineteen case vignettes in which the psychotherapist has attempted to provide an experience for the patient that is designed to resolve maturational tasks.

In his review of the literature the author traces the development of the therapeutic role from Freud through Ferenczi, Rank, Adler, and Sullivan to Alexander and French in the 1940's and then to “Hyman Spotnitz, whose formulations have been one of the most significant contributions to the literature on the resolution of the narcissistic disorders (schizophrenia and other preoedipal and preverbal problems).”

Strean divides his book into six chapters, including an epilogue on the mature adult. The six chapters are “Early Infancy”; Learning and Training”; “The Family Romance”; “Socialization”; “The Stormy Years of Puberty”; and “Adolescence.” In each chapter he describes the maturational needs, dysfunctions, and interventions necessary for the child (patient) to successfully progress to the next level of development. In the epilogue on the mature adult the author explores the many interpretations and multifaceted applications of maturity.

The tradition of linking the concepts of psychoanalysis and sexuality with literature was established by Freud when he borrowed from Sophocles the name for the most famous of his discoveries, the oedipus complex. Freud turned to the great masterworks of literature not only because he believed that they contained profound psychological truths but also because at that time little clinical material existed in the scientific literature with which to illustrate his evolving theoretical concepts.

In this book Norman Kiell attempts a synthesis of the stages of psychosexual development and literature. He systematically describes the principles of the psychology of sex and illustrates them with fictional passages. In doing so he avoids both literary pornography and the clinical drabness often prevalent in the scientific literature. The sexual phenomena are illustrated by the fictional work of over one hundred and fifty authors from the Apocrypha and Chaucer through Rabelais to Mailer and Vidal.

Selwyn Brody

Selwyn Brody  

Research evaluation in the treatment of schizophrenia has been largely neglected. The project in research evaluation which is the subject of this book began in 1970 at the National Institutes of Mental Health where it was given the highest priority. The impetus came from the psychotropic drugs which were responsible for a historic rate of discharge of schizophrenic patients from state hospitals in the 1960s, and which made the therapy of schizophrenia appear headed for extinction.

An alarming decline in the prestige of psychoanalytic training and teaching occurred as easier and faster methods promised more for less. A surge of interest in organicity was marked by accelerated research in genetics, brain biochemistry, and by a continuous stream of psychopharmacological remedies. Lithium was hailed as the third revolution in psychiatry. These events accounted for the defection of experienced psychiatrists, disillusioned with intensive psychotherapy.

But these drugs did not prove to be a biochemical solution. The wholesale release of patients was followed by a stampede of readmissions, the “revolving door” phenomenon. Community and family resources were not able to cope with released patients who were leading more impoverished lives than they had in the hospitals.

Joyce Bockar, psychiatrist, is a lecturer in the Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine, and is on the staff of Stamford Hospital where she is co-director of the inpatient unit, and clinical director of the Drug Liberation Program.

Bockar recognizes correctly that an increasing number of patients in need of counseling or psychotherapy are being treated by nonmedical professionals. She feels, however, that psychriatrists, because of their medical training, are consciously and unconsciously more alert to cues that some medical or organic disease process may be responsible for a patient's complaint. The aim of her book is to teach nonmedical professionals more about differential diagnosis and patients' medical illnesses. Her hope with this “primer” is that nonmedical practitioners, given a little more “medical intelligence,” will be better able to detect those signs in patients that signal the requirement for referral to a physician.

E. D.  

Paul Wachtel challenges the commonly held assumption that psychoanalysis and behaviorism are fundamentally irreconcilable models of personality and treatment. Wachtel points out the significant but seldom acknowledged commonalities between the two approaches; and he presents their important differences as valuable and complementary viewpoints on how to understand and treat maladaptive life patterns, rather than as a reflection of basic incompatibility.

The first chapters provide an exposition of the basic features of psychodynamic and behavioral thought. Wachtel reviews and makes fresh observations on the work of Freud, Sullivan, Dollard & Miller, Wolpe and the social learning theorists. Wachtel integrates the critical role of childhood in development with the behavioral point of view and proposes that these early events must be confirmed by a complex set of feed-back mechanisms which require the cooperation of other people and events. In his theory of treatment he presents an active-intervention psychodynamic perspective which combines a number of seemingly diverse approaches.

Rabkin's book undertakes to educate mental health workers in a variety of treatment strategies designed to provide brief and symptomatic treatment for a wide range of mental disorders found in clinic and private practice. Rabkin finds that traditional long-term therapy is neither an efficient nor desirable method for dealing with the vast majority of mental health problems. His book outlines the assumptions and practices of his approach. He describes the patient's role in therapy, deals with the problem of the compliant patient, and details the “healing fictions” of the therapist's role.

Hypnosis, relaxation techniques, reverse psychology, symptom substitution and small group or family therapy are discussed at length.

Richard Friedman

Richard Friedman

Richard Friedman  

The American Psychiatric Association Task Force on Nomenclature and Statistics has completed and distributed for field testing a draft edition of the new DSM. This is not so much a review of the new DSM-III as a preview, and it is written not from the perspective of the manual's usefulness for medical psychiatry but from the position of psychoanalysis as an independent mental health discipline. A distinction between psychiatry and psychoanalysis is important in discussing the DSM-III because, while many psychiatrists and some analytic institutes assert a special relationship between medicine and psychoanalysis, with this book the American Psychiatric Association has withdrawn its claim to psychoanalysis.

The diagnostic category “neurosis” has been eliminated from the DSM-III. This represents more than a shift in nomenclature. The editors of the DSM-III are proposing a fundamental overhauling of the intellectual foundations of psychiatry. The issue for the DSM-III editors is the intellectual viability of psychoanalysis, not only as a treatment modality, but also as a scientific system for understanding and diagnosing all mental functions.

The editor and one of his colleagues, Steven Jaffe, begin with an historical overview of psychopharmacology, then offer a collection of papers contributed by others. These papers discuss aspects of childhood and adolescent psychopharmacology of special concern to the editor.

Specific drug treatments of major clinical syndromes are described in considerable detail, along with cautions against using drug therapy as a replacement for, rather than an adjunct to, other treatment procedures. In addition, there are extensive discussions on classification of substances, mechanisms of action, and the relationship between drugs and childhood development—critical information that should contribute to a decrease in the misuse of psychopharmacologic drugs. Drug study methodology and drug treatment of the various states and special syndromes are also discussed.

The contributing authors take a basically conservative view of drug treatment with young people, stressing careful evaluation and specific, rather than general application. Specific indications and realistic expectations for drug treatment are clearly spelled out so that children who need drugs may be appropriately treated.

This one-volume reference book, intended primarily for child psychiatrists, pediatricians, and family practitioners who treat children for behavioral, psychological and developmental disturbances, should also be a valuable reference tool for the allied professions.

The aim of this book is to offer an “introductory teaching text” to practitioners in the field of family therapy. The first part of this text is devoted to a discussion of prevailing theories of marital and family treatment and to a review of individual, group and developmental dynamics. The second part of the book describes Skynner's and his wife's clinical work with families with many case illustrations and with especial reference to the treatment method of his choice—conjoint therapy. His stated approach is “group analytic” and he draws “heavily on the fruit of others” (intro. xii), mainly S.H. Foulkes and J.E. Bell, as well as on his personal group analysis.

Chapters six, seven, eight, and Appendix A, deal with the subjects of marriage, sexuality and family life, and summarize psychoanalytic theories on normal development and the family. They are illuminating and scholarly, and make valuable reading for students and practitioners. A description and discussion of modern psychoanalysis would have greatly enriched the usefulness of these chapters.

The author examines the bases of women's behavior, describes common misconceptions and shows how psychological findings have refuted them. As part of an historical overview, she discusses the psychoanalytic works of Freud, his disciples, and his critics.

The substance of the book is an ontogenetic analysis of the entire life cycle of women. The author begins by clarifying what is known about the biological determinants of behavior. The material on sex differences in infancy and early childhood is enhanced by the most recent data. The author further examines the development of the female by demonstrating how children learn and how social influences seriously affect behavior. The text pertaining to female adulthood includes full treatment of alternative lifestyles and the roles of housewife and mother. The chapter on variations from the norm takes up female emotional disorders, delinquency and crime.

Ideal Marriage

To say that there is a psychoanalytic view of marriage suggests that psychoanalysts have a specific opinion on the nature of marriage. Marriage is not a new institution, but the form it takes has constantly changed. Nevertheless, in any age, regardless of how revolutionary, people long for an ideal marriage.

That ideal is contained in the story of Philemon and Baucis. Ancient Greece was full of unrest and no one wanted to take in strangers, so when the gods Zeus and Hermes disguised themselves as travelers they had trouble finding lodging for the night. Even if people had known who they were, they might have been unwelcome; because the gods of antiquity were jealous, they instigated wars, struggled for power, undermined marriages, traded wives, and had love affairs. But these gods in disguise were finally given shelter by an impoverished elderly couple, Philemon and Baucis. In the morning when the gods departed, they revealed their identities and said that in return for the lodging they would fulfill whatever wish these two old people had. Philemon and Baucis had a short marital conference and answered, “If you please, see to it that we die at the same moment so that neither one of us will be left alone. That's all we want.” At that moment the gods turned them into two giant trees, so that they would grow forever, their leaves forever whispering to each other.

I cannot conceive of an emotional disturbance that does not contain a poblem in relationship, since my definition of normality entails creativity in forming relationships. If one cannot do that, then one cannot have a marriage. So the way to treat mantal disturbances is to treat the individual psychopathology. Part of normahty is the capacity of two people to get together.

I would treat a disturbance in a relationship in the same way that I would treat any other emotional disturbance. In other words, I would always deal with the indivdual transference neurosis. Instincts are object-seeking. Patients come and the analyst is the object and therefore they seek to form a relationship with he analyst. It may be oral, it may be anal, or it may be genita depending on what the particular psychopathology is, but they will form a relationship. Now, of course, according to psychoanalytic theory the relationship they form will replicate the relationship they formed with their primary objects. We are driven to repeat by unconscious forces. A patient's relationship to me is going to be somewhat different from his relationship to his mate, to his parents, or to his butcher, but it will still be driven by similar unconscious forces, so on the whole it will be a repetition of the problem.

This is why I believe that there is not very much to be gained by listening to a patient talk about what her husband does.

The Conflict Between the Patient's and Analyst's Reality in Classical and Modern Psychoanalysis

Gerald Lucas

Gerald Lucas

112 West 87th Street
New York, N.Y. 10024

Gerald Lucas  

Modern psychoanalysts frequently tell their patients that all the patient has to do is tell the story of his life and the rest is up to the analyst. This division of labor is based upon accepting in treatment a patient who may be an emotional infant and who needs to be completely taken care of while he is on the analytic couch. The assumption of a larger share of the therapeutic burden by the analyst corresponds to an improvement in technique of treatment over that of Sigmund Freud (1904) who designated certain kinds of patients as unsuitable for analysis, and over that of contemporary classical analysts who continue to require that their patients be capable of a working or therapeutic alliance with the analyst. In line with his appraisal of his technical achievement, Freud recommended a trial period to determine whether a given patient was or was not suitable for analysis. Certain patients, however, escaped screening and others were continued in treatment on an experimental basis. If, in the course of treatment during this trial period, the analyst makes interventions which the patient experiences as insulting or damaging to his self esteem, the analyst is free to conclude that the patient was initially unsuitable for analytic treatment.

In discussing the contra-indications for psychoanalytic treatment, Otto Fenichel (1945) considered the possession by the patient of a reasonable and cooperative ego to be of “the greatest practical importance” (p. 577).

A broken appointment, as other manifest behavior, often has quite different meanings to different patients. In addition, it may have different significance for the same patient at various phases in treatment. This is still more complicated in child treatment since the child's broken appointment may often be a manifestation of the parent's disguised feelings about the therapy.

Many successfully helped families have had a large number of broken appointments during the course of therapy. Yet we often fail with other families who reveal their unfortunate treatment experiences by suddenly breaking appointments. It would appear that a statistical approach offers little or no possibility of establishing (1) the underlying meaning of the broken appointment to the individual family; (2) the meaning of the broken appointment to the individual members of the family; and (3) the meaning of the broken appointment with regard to the process of therapy.

Some patients give several days' notice before canceling. Others telephone to cancel on the day of their interview, yet allow enough time to change their mind. Still others may telephone after their appointment time and offer an explanation for their absence. Some fail to keep their appointments and may not telephone at all. When contacted by their therapist, they may say they “forgot.” A few of the patients who break off contact abruptly may be unreachable by telephone and letter, and just disappear from treatment.

The Modern Analytic Teacher In an Elementary School

Dolores Welber

Dolores Welber  

The common feature of the roles of mother, teacher, and analyst is that in each there is a sequence of how people feel, think, and talk to each other. Study reveals that feelings come first in every relationship. How one relates to these feelings either helps or hinders one's role performance. When the teacher has been trained to use feelings productively, she may experiment with introducing this kind of education into her work with children. Such an experiment took place at an elementary school called The Studio on Eleventh Street.

The Studio was founded in 1971 as a laboratory school for the integration and demonstration of modern psychoanalytic techniques and modern educational concepts and developments. It is an early childhood and elementary school; students range in age from three to fourteen. We also work with children from fourteen to eighteen on a tutorial basis.

The special identity of the Studio centers on three features: vertical age grouping, work with family dynamics, and work with resistances.

Most elementary schools employ only horizontal grouping: children of the same approximate age are taught together. Using the analogy of family life, we do both vertical and horizontal grouping. Students from three to fourteen are in certain classes together, for example, in swimming, kitchen science, discussion groups, and general work periods.

Modern Psychoanalysis and the Teacher**

William Kirman

310 East 65th Street
New York, N.Y. 10021

William Kirman  

Introduction

Modern psychoanalysis, with greater flexibility than classical analysis and a more sophisticated structure than other psychotherapies, is ideally suited for application to the classroom. With certain modifications in the analytic model and some elaboration in technique, modern psychoanalysis is extremely useful in helping students on the road to emotional maturity. The application here envisioned calls upon the teacher to sustain a sensible role in the cognitive development of the student while at the same time promoting emotional growth in the classroom. Abandonment of the curriculum is not advocated since it is not our goal to encourage emotionally healthy but intellectually deficient students.

When modern psychoanalysis is correctly applied to the ongoing classroom situation, both students and teachers should accelerate their intellectual and emotional growth. While classes in emotional education are valuable and should be included in the curriculum as separate courses, our aim is more broadly defined. We do not advocate a simple application of group therapy nor a special class in emotional education for students in a school or college setting.

Hattie Rosenthal

1950 S. Ocean Drive

Hattie Rosenthal  

The Dream Message

Freud hinted at the possibility that dreams convey messages. Spotnitz and Meadow (1976) have expanded the idea that the manifest dream content carries a message from the preverbal unconscious to the conscious while the associations carry the message from a later period.

One could ask why the message is conveyed in an unintelligible form. There are good reasons. It is as if the id would say: “Take me or leave me. I come in disguise, by dream, so that you (the ego) can decide whether you want to decode my message or push it back into oblivion.” The outcome depends on whether the dreamer needs to keep his neurosis and its secondary gain or is ready to grow out of it. The message from the unconscious may be deciphered in cooperation with the dream analyst if doing so will resolve a resistance.

Understanding the Message

If a withdrawn person dreams: “I saw a group of hilarious people and felt bitter envy,” the question it raises in the analyst's mind is, “Why not join them?”

Vamik Volkan, a faculty member of the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute, has written a clinical study illustrating his treatment of patients who rely heavily on primitive splitting as a defensive function of the ego, rather than on repression. Most of the patients he describes are either psychotic, borderline, or narcissistic personalities. The book is one of the most recent contributions to,

and illustrations of, object-relations theory at work, which, according to Volkan is “of enormous help toward understanding these particular patients.”

In the forward, Otto Kernberg accepts Volkan's acknowledgment of his reliance on Kernberg's own theoretical concepts. He places this current work alongside those of psychoanalytic ego psychologists and object-relations theorists such as Erikson, Jacobson, Mahler, Fairbairn, Winnicott, Bowlby, Klein, Sullivan, and Parsons. In addition to demonstrating a flexible approach to treatment, Volkan makes original contributions to theory with his observations and discussions of emotional flooding, transitional object relations, and affect theory from a clinical viewpoint. Volkan's book is valuable reading since it raises important theoretical issues concerning the etiology of these illnesses and their treatment; it suggests a perspective about the theoretical developments within psychoanalysis; and it assists the modern psychoanalytic reader by further defining what modern psychoanalysis is.

Volkan confirms once again that these patients are treatable. However, whether the illnesses are the result of too little love or too much hate in their development (or some combination of entirely different causative factors) cannot be determined. Also, it seems confirmed that the relationship with the therapist is of importance in the treatment. By means of consistent interpretation of the defensive style of the patient's fragmented ego, the patient is taught gently and acceptingly that his perceptions, judgments, and approach to living are wrong and that change in the direction of accepting the analyst's perceptions, judgments, and approaches to living will either merit the analyst's love or avoid the analyst's hate. Nowhere in the clinical illustrations does there appear to be facilitation of the full verbal expression of hate toward the analyst, a regular part of the analysis when conducted by the modern analyst. Instead of working to resolve the resistances to expressing verbally, and only verbally, the transference feelings to the analyst Volkan consistently avoids placing himself directly in the path of the patients' feelings by interpreting the projective/introjective defenses in order to accomplish the internalization of the analyst as a “new and stable” figure and thus establish a “reality base.

While traditional patients feel it is sufficient to simply lie on their backs and say everything, modern analysands are highly motivated to develop further techniques for being successfully treated. This paper is a summary of recent developments.

Starting Treatment

Effectiveness at being a patient starts with the first phone call. Analysts have many resistances to giving and maintaining treatment. The analyst may name a very high fee, have no time right now, or try to refer the patient elsewhere. It is best to be unhesitatingly cooperative in this early phase. When asked, patients should say that they can come any time. They should find out what fee the analyst likes to charge and offer to pay it.

Selecting an Analyst

This selection from Lacan's works includes nine articles which originated as lectures to fellow analysts or students: “The mirror stage as formative of the function of the I”; “Aggressivity in psychoanalysis”; “The function and field of speech and language in psychoanalysis”; “The Freudian thing”; “The agency of the letter in the unconscious or reason since Freud”; “On a question preliminary to any possible treatment of psychosis”; “The direction of the treatment and the principles of its power”; “The signification of the phallus”; “The subversion of the subject and the dialectic of desire in the Freudian unconscious”.

Jacques Lacan, generally considered the most influential French thinker since Sartre, is primarily a practicing psychoanalyst. He is especially concerned with the training of analysts. I assembled an “English” class in the spring semester of 1972 in an effort to employ and examine theory and techniques drawn from modern psychoanalysis in teaching. The class was made up of seven eleventh and twelfth grade boys who shared a reputation for being the most undisciplined underachievers in the school. Owing to their extreme resistance to the usual mode of learning, they had systematically alienated themselves from regular classes. They were noted for consistently poor grades and failures. They had marked intolerance for any frustration, and frequently they would be reported to the office for such unruly and disruptive behavior as fighting and cursing. They were freqently absent, and the teachers, for the most part, welcomed their absence with a sense of relief. Prior to this term each of these students had been suspended from regular classes for a variety of infractions at least once, and most were chronic suspendees. As they were all in the eleventh and twelfth grades, English was the primary class requirement in their programs. At this point they had completed the basic requirements for the general course of study for a high school diploma and were completing their elective subjects and English to finish school.

The decision to place them in this English class was determined by their behavior, which could only be described as resistive.

It is commonly held that the most intimate relationship in life is the one that exists between a mother and her infant at the breast. Although the infant has not mastered language, other channels for communication seem to suffice. It is also said that in marriage one may find the second most intimate relationship in life. It might be argued that marriage offers superior opportunities for intimacy to the mother-child kind, in that new skills learned in maturity can be used to avoid the pitfalls an infant's relationship is subject to when conflicting emotions are experienced.

For those who have successfully negotiated the developmental stages, marriage may provide intimate emotional contact. However, since marriage is a relationship in which needs from various stages in the development of one person interact with those of another, fixation or regression in either partner prevents the spontaneous enjoyment of the relationship, and instead provides a breeding ground for repetitions of unresolved emotional conflicts from the past. As such conflicts begin to interfere with the relationship, one or both partners may seek outside help.

Adults usually come to psychoanalytic treatment because they cannot achieve the goals they set for themselves in marriage or in other aspects of living. Some arrive complaining about the quest for a mate. Others are avoiding commitments or asking whether they should marry, or whom they should marry.

137 Riverside Drive

Richard Friedman  

I taught world history in an urban community college for several years. The courses were part of a core of compulsory subjects but were unusual in that each history instructor had freedom to create his own syllabus and course structure. The administration granted this freedom to the history faculty, I think, in recognition of a frustrating situation. The students did not like courses in subjects having no immediate applicability to their career training and for the most part saw history as the most irrelevant of the compulsory courses; the history faculty did not like teaching students who felt history was irrelevant. So the students were frustrated, the faculty was frustrated, and the administration was frustrated from hearing complaints from students and faculty. The administration dealt with its frustration by letting each instructor teach what and how he wanted.

This probably added to faculty frustration by giving an increased share of the blame for student learning failures to the individual instructors. And failures there were: half of all students beginning World History I never finished the semester. As students were seldom assigned to the same instructor for both semesters of the world history sequence, each instructor had ample opportunity to observe the results of his colleagues' approaches to teaching history.

Emotional factors have been linked to cancer for centuries, and more studies continue to appear on the subject. Extreme skepticism prevails against the acceptance of emotions in the “most organic of all organic diseases.” In Psychosomatic Medicine in the Seventies: An Overview (Lipowski, 1977), several articles on emotional factors in cancer are described, but there is no reference to psychotherapy.

Although evidence for stress-induced tumors in laboratory mice has been demonstrated, proof of emotional factors causing cancer in humans seems unlikely in the foreseeable future. Despite the priority accorded to tangible carcinogenic factors, current investigations do include the psychological in the list of predictive factors. In a long range psychosocial study on medical school freshmen it was found that those who developed cancer had given a history of family alienation (Thomas, 1973).

Emotions are in the mainstream of the vast research on brain function. The major psychoses, mood, memory, affects, impulses, dreams, fantasy and even thought are seen as associated with biochemical processes. It is out of date to regard emotions as unreal abstractions. All psychic experiences and attitudes, including faith, belief, hope, love and hate coincide with real neuroelectric and chemical events in the nervous system, especially at the synaptic junctions. Researchers promise exciting new discoveries in the accelerating field of neurotransmissions and neuroinhibitions (Lester, 1977).

General Medicine and the Psychoanalyst

Carl McGahee

Carl McGahee

300 Riverside Drive
New York, N.Y. 10025

Carl McGahee  

How much general medicine should a psychoanalyst know? Unfortunately, this question has become a political football with extremists polarized into opposing camps: those claiming that medical knowledge is completely irrelevant to psychoanalysis and those maintaining that only medical doctors should be psychoanalysts.

Perhaps the question should be phrased differently. Is it at all useful for the psychoanalyst to have some familiarity with the biological functioning of the body and the ways such functioning can become deranged in some forms of illness? Expressed thusly, the issue might be rescued from territorial disputes among competing disciplines.

The thesis of this essay is that such knowledge can be valuable to the psychoanalyst in several ways. The most obvious one is in sensitizing the analyst to problems needing medical attention. The dread of every analyst medical and non-medical alike, is the “psychogenic” headache which turns out to be a brain tumor. On the other hand, it is impractical and often countertherapeutic to send a patient to a physician everytime the patient reports a new wrinkle on an old symptom.

Some sophistication in medical matters can also be useful to the psychoanalyst in communicating with a physician about a patient's coexisting illness.

An intial contact and interview between patient and analyst in modern analysis differs in many ways from an initial contact and interview in classical psychoanalysis. Some similarities also exist. In the following discussion these differences and similarities in theory and practice will be highlighted and a summary of a modern psychoanalytic first interview will be presented as an illustration.

The first rules laid out by Freud (1912, 1913) for practicing analysts were based on his conviction that to take on the treatment of the schizophrenias or narcissistic disorders was a gross error of judgment. He believed that an analyst who undertakes to treat such cases “has committed a practical error; he has been responsbile for wasted expenditure and has discredited his method of treatment. He cannot fulfill his promise of cure.” A less pessimistic view of the psychoanalytic treatment of severe mental disorders is now emerging (Searles, 1965; Arieti, 1974).

While the definition of psychoanalysis as “any line of investigation which takes transference and resistance as the starting point of its work” remains the same, the rules and advice of classical analysis, as gleaned from Freud's early papers, differ in several important instances from those of the present-day modern analyst.

Dr. Meadow addressed herself to the modern psychoanalytic view of resistance to marital intimacy. All three participants related marital failure to unsuccessfully resolved object relations with mothering figures during the first years of life, when wishes and fears revolve around security, intimacy and autonomy. The Narcissistic Condition: A Fact of our Lives and Times. Ed. by Marie Coleman Nelson. Foreword by Benjamin Nelson. New York: Human Sciences Press, 1977. 300 pp.

Murray Sherman

Murray Sherman

Murray Sherman  

Few concepts have been as forcefully thrust to the fore of psychoanalytic theory and practice in recent years as that of narcissism. Marie Nelson's timely volume addresses a crucial challenge to both clinical practice and the comprehension of contemporary society. Benjamin Nelson's foreword makes this reciprocal relationship between the clinical and the social incisively clear.

Ann B. Johnson provides insight into the narcissism of alienated students, and Joel Emanuel investigates the enormous demands upon the teacher of such pupils. Samuel Rubin raises critical theoretical questions regarding the relationship of narcissism to masochism and aggression.

In a lively and imaginative chapter, Hyman Spotnitz presents a fantasied course of modern analysis with the original Narcissus of antiquity, and he supplies the actual dialogue that might ensue were that tragic youth to find his way to the analytic couch. It is surprising how much contemporary reality Spotnitz is able to inject into this dialogue across a gulf of two thousand years.

Evelyn Abrams

Evelyn Abrams

Evelyn Abrams  

This book of thirty-one previously published articles spans the period 1958-1972 and deals with the study and treatment of the whole range of preoedipal disorders. Peter Giovacchini, one of the analysts who find that the narcissistic patient can develop a transference and is thus amenable to psychological treatment, turns to classical psychoanalysis as offering the most optimistic approach. The formulations presented, although they may require future change, provide “some organization and guideline to what otherwise would appear to be a chaotic psychic morass.”

Within the framework of ego psychology Giovacchini uses a wealth of clinical material to provide a microscopic examination of ego development and structure and its efficient and pathological adaptations to reality with special emphasis on impaired identity sense. Important developmental concepts are investigated: how the crucial mothering experience affects psychic structure and object relationships; how maturational failures are reflected in several regressed states and in unresolved infantile symbiosis; how aggression appears in adaptive and disruptive aspects. Marriage is explored as a special type of object relationship; a section deals with psychic operations and ego states in severe psychosomatic disorders.

Part IV deals exclusively with various “Clinical and Technical Issues.

This book is to be highly recommended to both the experienced analyst and the beginning analyst. As Kernberg states in his preface, “The book presents a systematic analysis of borderline conditions—their psychopathology, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment.” To this reviewer, the high points are Kernberg's excellent, extensive description and development of the nature of the borderline personality. With great care and skill he discusses the differential diagnosis of the various types of characterological disturbances and clearly distinguishes among them. Kernberg reserves the term borderline personality organization to describe those patients having a stable pathological personality organization.

Harold Richman

Harold Richman

Harold Richman  

This entire volume is based on two premises. The first is that the fairy tale represents a basic struggle against severe difficulties which are overcome if one steadfastly meets, adjusts to, and masters all obstacles. This concept is presented repeatedly to the child in fairy tales as an intrinsic part of human existence. The second premise is that the child's need for magic enables him to conceptualize, via fairy tales, the emergence of good over bad as coming to fruition. The child can trust what the fairy tale says because it is consistent with his own world.

Bettelheim stresses the importance of externalization on the part of the child. In this, the fairy tale permits unusual clarity in the fantasy because “Long, long ago,” or “Once upon a time,” permits a safe and neutral ground for externalization. Since the fairy tale is presented in the language of symbols, the child can externalize not on the basis of tangible facts, but through the symbolic meaning that he attaches to them.

Bettelheim provides a logical and entertaining approach to the fairy tale as a psychological factor aiding the growth of the child.
